catalog_quote: 1.6.0 Okrika Orthography and Tonal System. Wákịrịkẹ̀ is tonal like other Ịjọ languages. The pitch of the voice makes a difference to the meaning of words, even when they are spelt in the same way. Often tones change pronunciation of words and sentences depending on the context in which these words are used. Therefore Wákịrịkẹ̀ words are tone-marked in order not to make it difficult for anybody who wants to know what meaning is intended. Okrika has five tones as listed below. [Table 1.4 Types of tones in Okrika:] 1. Low tone is marked with 2. High tone is marked with ´ 3. Down-step is marked with ¯ 4. Rising tone is marked with ˇ 5. Falling tone is market [sic] with ˆ. new_statements.rule_in_words: Kirike is a tone language (H, L, downstep; rising and falling contours on some syllables). No source opened says anything about word stress; none states a stress position. Corroborated by Blench's note in Sika/Blench 2005 p. xiii: 'Kịrịkẹ has a relatively restricted tone-system, distinguishing High, Low and Downstep, like many Ịjọ and Igbo lects.'
new_statements.exceptions: Wakama lists tone patterns LL, HH, HD, HL, LH, LR, F, LLF on words (p. 14). Sika's dictionary preface (p. v-vi) uses 'stress' loosely for the tone marks and calls downstep the 'middle stress', explicitly not 'a hard and fast rule'; this is orthographic tone marking, not word stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (tone-marked citation forms in a wordlist/dictionary); Wakama's variety is the Okrika of Wakirike/Okrika town (the mixed Okrika-Igbo lects of Ogan-ama etc. are treated separately); tone marks 'change.. depending on context', i.e. phrase-level tone processes exist (cf. Kalabari downdrift/downstep in Harry 2003).
new_statements.identity_note: Both opened sources describe the Okrika (Wakirike) of Okrika town and Ogu/Bolo LGAs, Rivers State = kiri1254 [okr]; Wakama 1999 treats the Okrika-Igbo mixed lects of Ogan-ama, George-ama etc. (Kirikeni-Igbonaye) as a separate mixed language, not as Kirike proper. Sika's dictionary marks some entries '(Ogu dialect)'. The earlier scan's named source Horton 1962 is an anthropological article on Kalabari (kala1381), not a Kirike description.

sources.note: Blench p. xiii 'Tones': 'Kịrịkẹ has a relatively restricted tone-system, distinguishing High, Low and Downstep, like many Ịjọ and Igbo lects' (low unmarked, ´ high, ¯ downstepped high). Sika's own pronunciation key p. v uses the word 'stress' for the three tone marks (high, low, level/downstep) and p. vi calls downstep 'middle stress'. No word-stress rule.
